#ai #tech #coding #student #university
content.transcript: If I started from scratch, this is how I would really learn coding in 2026. First, learn Python. It's easy, you can build basically anything with it, and once you know Python, every other programming language is easier to pick up. But a theory, you can do the Harvard CS50 course. It's free and it teaches you how code actually works. In parallel, you can do the free code compitons certificate, so you're actually coding from day one. Once you got the basics down, you should immediately start applying them to small projects. For that, you can visit the GitHub repo, build your own eggs, and pick out a project that you like. Most of the projects can be done in just a couple of days, and I would recommend doing at least one a week. Once the projects get bigger, I would also start to pick up on things like system, design, and version control with Git. For that, you can check out this tutorial on version control, and the system design primer repo on GitHub. And in 2026, you can't skip AI, so finish with Google's machine learning crash course. It's free and it covers all the basics, just enough to understand what's actually going on. You can pair that with Anthropics AI fluency course, so you know how to actually work with models like Cloud on your projects. And yes, AI can definitely write most of the code for you in 2026. But the people shipping actually work in projects are still the ones who understand what's going on. AI makes you faster, but it doesn't replace understanding. Comment code and I'll send you the full roadmap with every resource. Good luck and follow for more.

knowledge.title: 2026 Coding Roadmap
knowledge.summary: A comprehensive roadmap for learning to code in 2026, emphasizing Python, foundational theory, project-based learning, and AI literacy. The approach balances theoretical knowledge with practical application and version control.
key_takeaways: Python is the recommended starting language due to its versatility and ease of learning.
Combine theoretical learning with practical coding exercises from day one.
Consistent project building is essential for skill development.
AI tools should be used to increase speed, but they do not replace the need for deep understanding.
System design and version control are critical skills for larger projects.
best_practices: Learn Python first to make other languages easier to pick up.
Learn theory and practice coding in parallel.
Build small projects immediately after learning the basics.
Aim to complete at least one project per week.
Understand the underlying concepts rather than relying solely on AI.
mistakes_to_avoid: Do not skip learning about AI in 2026.
Do not rely on AI to replace your own understanding of code.
action_items: Study the system design primer repo on GitHub.
Take Google's machine learning crash course.
